frase_gancho.texto: An earth deity who does not hide on a base.

puente_narrativo.texto: From the myth of a defeated goddess, we move to another image tied to the earth: the deity carved on the base of the Coatlicue.

guion_corto.texto: Where does Tlaltecuhtli usually hide? Almost always below. Mexica sculptors carved her in relief on the underside of other works, pressed against the ground, as happens on the base of the Coatlicue. This sculpture is different: it is a freestanding figure, worked on all sides. Tlaltecuhtli is the Mexica deity of the earth. Some call her the Coatlicue of the Metro, but she is not Coatlicue. Look at the posture: she is squatting, with her legs bent as in childbirth, and claws extend from her hands and feet. The face is fleshless and the mouth opens, ready to swallow. On her chest she wears a necklace of hearts and hands. For the Mexica, the earth was a living being that gave food and received the dead. This sculpture puts that idea right in front of you.

guion_largo.texto:
Tlaltecuhtli is the Mexica deity of the earth, and she is almost always seen hidden away. Sculptors carved her in relief on the underside of other works, as happens on the base of the Coatlicue. That way she stayed pressed against the ground. This sculpture breaks with that custom. It is a freestanding figure, worked on all sides and made to be seen from the front.

Some call her the Coatlicue of the Metro, but she is not Coatlicue. She resembles that goddess because of the necklace of hearts and hands she wears on her chest. Still, her posture gives her away. She is squatting, with her legs spread and bent, in the position of a woman giving birth. Claws extend from her hands and her feet. The face is skeletal and the open mouth shows the teeth.

For the Mexica, the earth was a living being. Plants were born from it, and the dead returned to it. A creation myth tells that the world was water. Then Quetzalcóatl and Tezcatlipoca turned into serpents and tore the body of a monster called Tlaltecuhtli in two. With one half they made the sky and with the other the earth.

From the deity’s body sprang trees, flowers, springs and caves. But it is said that the earth wept at night and asked for blood and hearts in order to bear its fruits.

That is why this figure does not smile. She is the earth that nourishes and the earth that demands, brought together in a single image.

texto: Notice the posture of the figure, with its legs bent.
Look for the claws that tip the hands and feet of the figure.
Find the necklace of hearts and hands that hangs across the chest.

texto.pregunta: Myth: This sculpture is another Coatlicue.
texto.respuesta: Reality: It is popularly called the “Coatlicue of the Metro,” but it is Tlaltecuhtli, the Mexica deity of the earth. The Coatlicue is a different sculpture, and on its base Tlaltecuhtli is carved.
